Winterhouse
WIN-tur-hows
n. (the heated quarters of a palace; where Jehoiakim burned the word of God)
A compound of winter and house, rendering Hebrew beth hachoreph — the winter apartment of a great house, distinguished from the summer house, and warmed by a brazier on the hearth.

Biblical Definition

Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him. Jeremiah had dictated the whole of his prophecy to Baruch, and the roll was read in the temple, then to the princes, and at last brought to Jehoiakim. The detail of the fire is given before the scene because it is the instrument. When Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed. Three or four columns at a time, cut and burned, the king warm and unhurried, working through the word of God the way a man feeds a fire. Jeremiah adds that they were not afraid, nor rent their garments — a deliberate contrast with Josiah, Jehoiakim's own father, who had rent his clothes when the book was found. Amos names the winter house in a judgment: I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish. God's answer to Jehoiakim was to have the roll written again, and more added — the word he burned came back longer. Comfort is not the sin here; the winter house is only a room. What Jeremiah records is a man so settled in it that he could burn Scripture without a tremor.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a house or apartment occupied in winter; a warmed dwelling, as distinguished from a summer residence.

expand to see more

WINTER-HOUSE, n. A house or apartment to be occupied in winter.

HEARTH, n. A pavement or floor of brick or stone in a chimney, on which a fire is made.

ROLL, n. A volume; a book formed of a sheet of paper or parchment rolled up.

PENKNIFE, n. A small knife used for making and mending pens.

CONSUME, v.t. To destroy by separating the parts of a thing; to burn up; to waste.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 36:22 — "Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him."

Jeremiah 36:23 — "And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth."

Amos 3:15 — "And I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the LORD."

Isaiah 22:9 — "Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool."

Modern Corruption

Rejection of Scripture is imagined as a dramatic act of unbelief; Jeremiah shows it as a comfortable man with a penknife, unhurried, in a warm room, not even angry.

expand to see more

The scene is chilling precisely because it is so calm. Jehoiakim does not argue with the prophecy, does not summon scholars to refute it, does not rage. He listens to three or four leaves, cuts them off, and drops them in the fire, and repeats the procedure until the roll is gone. Jeremiah notes that the king and his servants were not afraid, nor rent their garments. Most rejection of God's word looks like this rather than like open blasphemy: a passage found unhelpful and quietly set aside, a doctrine retired as unsuited to the times, a text edited down to what the room will bear. The penknife is always small.

The answer God gave is worth as much attention as the offence. He told Jeremiah to take another roll and write all the former words again, and there were added besides unto them many like words. The word Jehoiakim burned came back longer, and it also came back with a sentence on him personally. Scripture has been burned, banned and edited in every century since and has outlasted every hearth. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew choreph (H2779), winter or harvest-time; ach (H254), a fire-pan or hearth; megillah (H4039), a roll or scroll; taar (H8593), a knife or razor.

expand to see more

Hebrew choreph (H2779) — winter; the season naming the heated apartment of a palace.

Hebrew ach (H254) — a brazier or hearth; the fire burning before the king.

Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, a scroll; the form in which Jeremiah's prophecies were written.

Hebrew taar (H8593) — a knife or razor; the penknife of a scribe, turned against the text.

Hebrew qara (H7167) — to rend; what Josiah did with his clothes, and what Jehoiakim did not.

Usage

"“the king sat in the winterhouse” — the setting given before the deed."

"“he cut it with the penknife” — three or four leaves at a time."

"“I will smite the winter house with the summer house” — Amos on the end of such comfort."
